overview.body:
**Śakti** (*shakti*) — Power, Energy, Divine Feminine · Power, ability, energy — the active power of a deity personified as his consort — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Power, Energy, Divine Feminine". The name means "Power, ability, energy — the active power of a deity personified as his consort"[^1].

**Śakti** belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is associated with power, energy, divine feminine.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Śakti** and serves its temple at [shakti.com](https://punicodex.com/shakti/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *shakti* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.
Rāmāyaṇa, Vālmīki; translated by Hari Prasad Shastri, 500 BCE.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Devanagari as **शक्ति**. Etymologically it means "Power, ability, energy — the active power of a deity personified as his consort"[^1].

Sanskrit Śakti, from the root śak 'to be able, to have power'; the dynamic feminine energy of the divine.

The ASCII form *shakti* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Śakti** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **s** → **Ś** — S with acute: palatal s
- **h** → **—** — Dropped
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **k** → **k** — Same
- **t** → **t** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same

The canonical temple for this name is served at **shakti.com**[^2].

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/shakti/** — Sanskrit Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Ś** — Initial character of the restored form Śakti.
- **akti** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Sanskrit tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'SHAKTI' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Sanskrit** — Śakti, the restored Unicode form of the name

Śakti is Tier 1 because the Sanskrit form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

original-script.body:
The name is preserved in Devanagari as **शक्ति**.[^1]

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

mythology.body:
The stories of **Śakti** circulate within the Sanskrit corpus, where the figure embodies power, energy, divine feminine.[^1]

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Śakti is attested in the canonical Sanskrit sources as a figure associated with power, energy, divine feminine.[^2]

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "Power, ability, energy — the active power of a deity personified as his consort" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Śakti** is the dynamic feminine power that animates every Hindu deity. Without his śakti, Śiva is a corpse; with her he creates, preserves, and destroys.[^1] She appears as Pārvatī, Durgā, Kālī, and countless local goddesses, each an expression of the same cosmic energy. Tantric traditions map the subtle body through cakras and channels as the geography of Śakti's ascent to union with Śiva at the crown.[^2]

sources.citation: Rāmāyaṇa, Vālmīki; translated by Hari Prasad Shastri, 500 BCE.

syncretism.body:
Śakti appears within the Sanskrit tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.[^1]

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[daksa|Dakṣa]], [[dhatr|Dhātṛ]], [[durga|Durgā]], [[ganesha|Gaṇeśa]], and [[ganga|Gaṅgā]].

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

cultural-legacy.body: Śakti continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Sanskrit tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes.[^1] Śakti worship underlies tantra, Śākta devotion, and goddess movements across South Asia and the diaspora.[^1]

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

meditation.body: Śakti embodies power, energy, divine feminine in the Sanskrit imagination. The name's restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make the figure recognizable in the source tradition.[^1]

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

vedic-references.body:
The **Devī Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.125)** is the earliest textual declaration of the Goddess as the supreme power underlying all gods, speech, and cosmic order.[^1] Vedic hymns to **Uṣas, Vāc, and Pṛthivī** provide the precedents for the later concept of Śakti as divine feminine energy.[^2]

The Devī Sūkta remains the charter text for Śākta theology.

sources.citation: Vedic hymns to Ushas, Vac, and Prithvi.

upanishads.body:
The **Devī Upaniṣad** and **Tripurā Upaniṣad** identify the Goddess with Brahman and describe her as the source, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.[^1] The **Muṇḍaka** and **Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣads** supply the Vedāntic language of power (*śakti*) through which the cosmos proceeds.[^2]

Śakti is therefore not a separate goddess but the dynamic aspect of the Absolute.

puranas.body:
The **Devī-Māhātmya** (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, chs. 81–93) narrates the Goddess's victories over Mahiṣāsura and other demons, establishing her as the warrior queen of the cosmos.[^1] The **Devī-Bhāgavata Purāṇa** and **Liṅga Purāṇa** develop the theology of Śakti as inseparable from Śiva.[^2]

These Purāṇas are the scriptural bedrock of Śākta worship.

mantras.body:
The **Mahāvidyā** mantras, **Durgā Saptaśatī** verses, and **Śrīvidyā** practices are the central sonic technologies of Śakti worship.[^1] The **Pañcadaśī** and **Ṣoḍaśī** mantras of the Śrīvidyā tradition are regarded as concentrated forms of the Goddess's own body and power.[^2]

Recitation (*japa*) and diagrammatic worship (*Śrīcakra*) transform sound into divine presence.
